title: Can, must, want, may
goal: Ask for help, ask permission, offer a hand and turn things down politely — and sort out the verbs that English squeezes into "can" and "may".
bekal: using *mogu, moram, hoću, želim, trebam, smijem* with the dictionary form after them
telling *ne moram* (don't have to) from *ne smijem* (mustn't)
asking for help and declining an invitation without sounding rude

dialogs.title: Dialogue — Papiri za boravišnu dozvolu
dialogs.intro: Budi has to apply for a residence permit, and the form is entirely in Bosnian. He gives up on line three and turns to the next desk.

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: Amina, možeš li mi pomoći? Samo pet minuta.
lines.id: Amina, can you help me? Just five minutes.
lines.literal: Amina, you-can whether to-me help? only five minute-gen-pl.

lines.speaker: Amina:
lines.id: Of course. What do you need?

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: Moram predati papire za boravišnu dozvolu, ali ne razumijem formular.
lines.id: I have to hand in the papers for my residence permit, but I don't understand the form.
lines.literal: I-must hand-in paper-acc-pl for residence-acc-f permit-acc, but not I-understand form-acc.

lines.speaker: Amina:
lines.text: Pokaži mi. Ovdje moraš napisati adresu, a ovdje datum rođenja.
lines.id: Show me. Here you write your address, and here your date of birth.
lines.literal: show to-me. here you-must write address-acc, and here date birth-gen.

lines.speaker: Amina:
lines.text: Gdje si rođen. Jakarta, zar ne?
lines.id: Where you were born. Jakarta, right?
lines.literal: where you-are born-m. Jakarta, isn't not?

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.id: Yes. Can I write in Latin letters?

lines.speaker: Amina:
lines.text: Možeš, naravno. Hoćeš li da idem s tobom u policiju?
lines.id: You can, of course. Do you want me to come with you to the police?
lines.literal: you-can, of-course. you-want whether that I-go with you-ins to police-acc?

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.id: Really? You don't have to, honestly.

lines.speaker: Amina:
lines.id: I want to. I'm off tomorrow anyway.

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: Hvala ti puno! Onda trebamo krenuti rano.
lines.id: Thanks so much! Then we need to leave early.
lines.literal: thanks to-you much! then we-need set-off early.

lines.speaker: Amina:
lines.text: Važi. U osam ispred zgrade. Samo nemoj zaboraviti pasoš!
lines.id: Deal. Eight o'clock outside the building. Just don't forget your passport!
lines.literal: it-holds. at eight in-front-of building-gen. only don't forget passport!

notes: **Every helping verb in this dialogue is followed by the dictionary form:** *moram predati*, *moraš napisati*, *mogu pisati*, *trebamo krenuti*, *nemoj zaboraviti*, *neću zaboraviti*. That is the standard pattern, and it works for all the verbs in the table below without exception.

***Hoćeš li da idem s tobom?* — a second pattern, just as correct.** Instead of the dictionary form, Bosnian can use *da* + a present-tense verb: *moram da idem* means the same as *moram ići*. You will hear both all day in Sarajevo. The *da* form is required when the subjects differ: *Hoćeš li da **idem** s tobom?* — you are the one who wants, I am the one who goes.

***Ne moraš* means "you don't have to", not "you mustn't".** English has exactly the same trap with *must not* vs *don't have to*, and the consequences can be big. "You mustn't" is *ne smiješ*. Compare: *Ne moraš doći* (no need to come) and *Ne smiješ doći* (you are not allowed to come).

***Važi!*** is the most common Bosnian word for agreeing to something — "OK, deal, sure". Literally "it holds". Its relatives: *U redu* (all right), *Dogovoreno* (agreed), *Nema problema*, and the most casual, *Može*.

**Getting a residence permit in Bosnia means dealing with *Služba za strance*.** They always ask for: *pasoš*, *prijava boravka* (address registration, done by your host within 24 hours of arrival), *ugovor o radu* (work contract) and *ljekarsko uvjerenje* (health certificate). Bring two photocopies of everything — the question *Trebate li kopiju?* can save you a whole extra trip.

grammars.title: Six helping verbs — and how they differ
body: English uses "can" for three different things: circumstances allow it, I have the skill, and I'm asking permission. Bosnian splits them up.

head: Dictionary form
ja
on / ona
Meaning
Example
rows: *Smijem li ući?* — May I come in?

after: ***Moći* vs *znati*.** *Ne mogu doći* = circumstances don't allow it (I'm busy, I'm ill). *Ne znam kuhati* = I don't have the skill. If you say *Ne mogu kuhati*, it means your kitchen is out of order, not that you're a bad cook.

***Htjeti* vs *željeti*.** *Hoću* is direct and everyday — at the café, in the shop, at home. *Želim* is softer and more formal; it is also used for wishes (*Želim ti sreću* — I wish you luck). In a restaurant the waiter asks *Šta želite?*, never *Šta hoćete?*

***Trebati* has two patterns, and the second is actually more common.** First: *Trebam pomoć* (I need help — the thing is accusative). Second: *Treba mi pomoć*, literally "help is needed to me" — here the thing becomes the subject and you become the receiver. *Treba mi odmor. Trebaju mi papiri.* The second pattern uses the dative, which comes in Unit 13.

**Learn the negatives as pairs:** *ne mogu* (can't), *ne smijem* (mustn't), *ne moram* (don't have to), *neću* (won't), *ne trebam* (don't need). Note that *neću* fuses into one word — the third and last verb to do so, after *nisam* and *nemam*.

grammars.title: Asking, offering, accepting, declining
body: Four social jobs that all use the same helping verbs. Learn the opening phrases whole — after that you just swap the verb at the end.
after: **A refusal in Bosnia almost always has three parts**: a word of regret (*nažalost*, unfortunately), a short reason (*moram raditi*) and an offer of another time (*može sutra?*). Saying just *ne* sounds cold — not because it is grammatically rude, but because here an invitation is an offer of friendship, not just a calendar slot.
***Rado* means "gladly"** and is the warmest answer to an offer. *Hoćeš li kafu? — Rado!* One word, and the whole conversation lifts.

***Hajde da…* is the easiest way to invite.** *Hajde da idemo na kafu. Hajde da probamo.* If you remember only one invitation pattern, make it this one — it works with any verb and needs no new forms.

***Molim te* and *molim vas* can be slipped in anywhere** and always soften things: *Možeš li mi, molim te, pomoći?* In Bosnian a longer request sounds more polite than a short one — much as "Could you possibly…" does in English.

blocks.text: Bosnian forms always use the same words, and almost all of them stand alone, without a sentence. Once you recognize these words, nearly any form becomes readable.

head: Lifesavers at the counter
English
rows: Excuse me, where is the counter for foreigners?
I need to hand in these papers.
*Ne razumijem ovaj formular. Možete li mi pomoći?*
I don't understand this form. Could you help me?
When can I pick up the document?
Do I have to pay a fee?
Do you speak English? I'm learning Bosnian.

blocks.title: One sentence that changes the mood at the counter
items: ***Izvinite, ja učim bosanski, pa govorim polako.*** — "Sorry, I'm learning Bosnian, so I speak slowly." Say it first, before the clerk can switch to broken English. The result is almost always the same: the tone softens and people start speaking more slowly, not more loudly.
The word *stranac* (foreigner) is not rude in Bosnia — it appears on counter signs and official forms. The feminine is *strankinja*.
